classification.difficultyReason: Extend acute-angle sine ordering to triangle angles through supplement comparisons and both directions of an equivalence, then transfer the ordering to sides using the sine rule.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Suppose $\angle A,\angle B\leq90^\circ$. With the aid of a diagram explain why
$$\angle A\leq\angle B\iff\sin(A)\leq\sin(B).$$

answer.short: For right triangles with hypotenuse $1$, the opposite side has length $\sin\theta$. As the acute angle increases, this side increases, so the stated equivalence holds, including equality.
answer.worked:
Draw two right triangles with a common initial ray and hypotenuses of length $1$, as shown. The vertical sides have lengths $\sin A$ and $\sin B$. On the quarter-circle of radius $1$, the height increases strictly as the angle increases from $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$. Thus the smaller angle has the smaller opposite side, and conversely. Equal angles give equal opposite sides. Hence
$$\angle A\leq\angle B\iff\sin A\leq\sin B.$$

spec.sourceRegion: Question 17(a); answer figure on teacher PDF page 13
spec.description: Two overlapping right triangles with a common initial ray and unit hypotenuses, illustrating a smaller and a larger acute angle. Illustrative coordinates are not numerical givens.
spec.mathematics: Unit hypotenuses make the perpendicular opposite sides equal to sin A and sin B; A is illustrated smaller than B.
spec.answerVisibility: Solution only; the student must supply a diagram.

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Hence, prove that
$$\angle A\leq\angle B\iff\sin(A)\leq\sin(B)$$
whenever $\angle A$ and $\angle B$ are (possibly obtuse) angles in a triangle.

answer.short: Use part (a), $A+B<180^\circ$ and $\sin(180^\circ-\theta)=\sin\theta$ to prove both directions, treating an obtuse angle through its acute supplement.
answer.worked:
Angles in a triangle satisfy $A+B<180^\circ$.

First suppose $A\leq B$. If $B\leq90^\circ$, part (a) gives $\sin A\leq\sin B$. If $B>90^\circ$, then $A<180^\circ-B<90^\circ$, so part (a) gives
$$\sin A<\sin(180^\circ-B)=\sin B.$$

Conversely, suppose $\sin A\leq\sin B$. If $A>90^\circ$, then $B<180^\circ-A<90^\circ$. Part (a) would give $\sin B<\sin(180^\circ-A)=\sin A$, a contradiction. Thus $A\leq90^\circ$. If $B\leq90^\circ$, part (a) gives $A\leq B$. If $B>90^\circ$, then $A\leq90^\circ<B$.

Therefore
$$A\leq B\iff\sin A\leq\sin B.$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Given $\triangle ABC$, prove that $a\leq b\leq c$ if and only if $\angle A\leq\angle B\leq\angle C$.

answer.short: The sine rule gives $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{\sin A}{\sin B}$. Thus $a\leq b$ is equivalent to $\sin A\leq\sin B$, and hence to $A\leq B$ by part (b). Apply the same argument to $b$ and $c$.
answer.worked:
By the sine rule,
$$\frac{a}{b}=\frac{\sin A}{\sin B}.$$
Since $b>0$ and $\sin B>0$,
$$\begin{aligned}
a\leq b&\iff\frac{a}{b}\leq1\\
a\leq b&\iff\frac{\sin A}{\sin B}\leq1\\
a\leq b&\iff\sin A\leq\sin B\\
a\leq b&\iff A\leq B.
\end{aligned}$$
The last equivalence follows from part (b). Similarly, $b\leq c$ if and only if $B\leq C$. Combining the two equivalences gives
$$a\leq b\leq c\iff A\leq B\leq C.$$
